question: What is the primary medical term for painful menstrual cramps?
explanation: Dysmenorrhea is the specific medical term used to describe painful menstruation that interferes with a woman's daily activities. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why do many women in Nigeria delay seeking care for severe menstrual pain?

options.A: Severe pain is often wrongly viewed as a normal part of being a woman
options.B: Traditional herbs completely cure all forms of pelvic pain
options.C: Hospitals charge very high fees specifically for menstrual cramps
options.D: Midwives are legally barred from discussing menstrual disorders

explanation: Cultural normalization of menstrual pain leads many women and families to suffer in silence without seeking professional medical help. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which chemical substance released by the endometrium is the primary cause of pain in primary dysmenorrhea?
explanation: Excessive prostaglandin production causes the uterus to contract strongly, reducing blood flow and resulting in crampy pain. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h2)

question: When does primary dysmenorrhea most commonly first appear in a young woman's life?

options.A: During menopause when hormone levels begin to fluctuate wildly
options.B: Shortly after ovulatory cycles become established following menarche
options.C: Years before her very first menstrual period begins
options.D: Only after she has given birth to her first child

explanation: Primary dysmenorrhea usually appears within the first year or two after a girl starts menstruating, once her cycles become regularly ovulatory. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common cause of secondary dysmenorrhea?
explanation: Primary hormonal fluctuation drives normal cycles and primary dysmenorrhea, whereas secondary dysmenorrhea is caused by distinct structural or inflammatory conditions like fibroids. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h3)

question: What clinical feature strongly points toward secondary dysmenorrhea rather than primary dysmenorrhea?

options.A: Normal pelvic examination findings with no uterine tenderness
options.B: Pain starting for the first time in a woman in her late thirties
options.C: Cramps lasting for only forty-eight hours during bleeding
options.D: Mild nausea accompanying the first day of menstruation

explanation: New-onset dysmenorrhea appearing later in life, well past adolescence, is a classic sign of an acquired secondary pelvic pathology. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is the very first step a midwife should take when evaluating a client presenting with painful periods?

options.B: Perform an immediate pregnancy test without asking questions
options.D: Take a detailed menstrual and medical history

explanation: A thorough history is the essential first step to understand the pain pattern and differentiate between primary and secondary causes. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why must a midwife always rule out pregnancy before starting medical treatment for pelvic pain?

options.A: Pregnant women never experience any form of pelvic or abdominal discomfort
options.B: Pregnancy completely cures all forms of primary and secondary dysmenorrhea
options.C: Many common pain medications and treatments can harm an early developing pregnancy
options.D: Hospitals in Nigeria prohibit giving any medication to women of childbearing age

explanation: Because NSAIDs and hormonal therapies can be teratogenic or cause complications, pregnancy must be ruled out first. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which class of medication is considered the first-line pharmaceutical treatment for primary dysmenorrhea?
explanation: NSAIDs directly target the production of prostaglandins, which are the main culprits behind primary dysmenorrhea pain. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h5)

question: How do combined oral contraceptive pills help reduce menstrual cramp pain?

options.A: By paralyzing the nerves that transmit pain signals to the brain
options.B: By suppressing ovulation and keeping the endometrial lining thin
options.C: By directly destroying uterine fibroids within the pelvic cavity
options.D: By permanently stopping all future menstrual cycles forever

explanation: Oral contraceptives prevent ovulation and reduce the thickness of the endometrium, which lowers the overall amount of prostaglandins produced. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h5)

question: What advice should a midwife give a client regarding when to take her prescribed NSAID for menstrual cramps?

options.A: Take the medication at the very onset of bleeding or right before pain starts
options.B: Wait until the pain becomes unbearable before taking any pill
options.C: Take the medication only after the menstrual period has completely ended
options.D: Take the pills exclusively during the middle of the menstrual cycle

explanation: Taking NSAIDs early prevents prostaglandins from building up and causing severe contractions, making pain control much more effective. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which of the following is a warning sign that requires a client with dysmenorrhea to seek immediate medical review?

options.A: Needing to rest for an hour on the first day
options.B: Mild fatigue on the first day of her period
options.C: A slight decrease in energy levels during menses
options.D: Sudden high fever and foul-smelling vaginal discharge

explanation: Fever and foul discharge suggest an underlying pelvic infection like PID, which needs urgent medical diagnosis and antibiotic treatment. [learn more](BMP310_U3_T2#BMP310_U3_T2_h6)
